bp: A knowledge graph is a store of connected facts: things are nodes, relations are links, and types or classes describe what kinds of things and links are allowed. A company, search engine, scientific database, or public data portal may use this structure to combine facts from many sources. The hard practical question is not only whether a graph contains many facts, but whether the graph is still healthy as it grows. Are related parts tied together or split into islands? Can users travel from one fact to another through meaningful links? Has the organizing scheme become too deep, too shallow, or inconsistent? MetriKG serves the maintenance side of this world. It is a web application for profiling static and evolving knowledge graphs from RDF files or SPARQL endpoints. Its purpose is to turn a large connected knowledge store into measurements that help people monitor quality, consistency, and interpretability over time.
wh: The difficulty is that graph quality is not visible from a single fact. A fact can be correct by itself while the graph around it becomes confusing. One part may grow dense while another becomes isolated. A new class may be added to the schema, meaning the organizing rules of the graph, but the actual data may not follow that new shape. Existing evaluation methods, as described in the abstract, often look at static graphs or track evolution only at the data level. That misses a second layer of change: the schema can also evolve. If the graph says what entities exist but quietly changes what types, hierarchies, or relation patterns are expected, then users may trust a map whose rules have shifted underneath them. MetriKG is hard because it must summarize both surface facts and deeper organization without reducing everything to one vague quality score.
naive: A smart beginner might load the graph, count how many facts it has, count how many entity types appear, and compare those totals across two dates. If the counts rise, the graph looks healthier. If some links disappear, it looks worse. That approach fails because size is not structure. A graph can gain many facts while becoming less connected. It can keep the same number of classes while making the class hierarchy deeper and harder to interpret. It can add data that obeys old rules poorly, or change schema rules while the data-level counts look stable. Simple counts tell that something changed, but not what kind of change happened or whether it threatens cohesion, connectivity, classification, or later use.
ap: MetriKG's central move is to treat a knowledge graph like an object that can be profiled from several angles rather than judged by one headline number. The application accepts graphs either as RDF files, which are files of subject-relation-object statements, or through SPARQL endpoints, which are query services for asking a graph what it contains. It then computes a broad set of metrics for both static graphs and graphs observed over time. Some metrics describe data-level structure, such as how connected or cohesive the graph is. Others describe schema-level structure, such as inheritance depth, meaning how many layers sit between broad classes and more specific classes. The important design choice is the pairing of levels. MetriKG does not only ask whether the facts changed. It also asks whether the rules and categories that give those facts meaning changed.
mech: The mechanism begins with an input knowledge graph. If the user provides an RDF file, MetriKG reads the stored statements directly. If the user provides a SPARQL endpoint, it queries the graph through the endpoint instead. From there, the application separates two views. The data-level view looks at the concrete fact network: which entities are present, which relation links connect them, and how those links create connected regions or isolated pieces. The schema-level view looks at the organizing layer: what classes, relation types, and inheritance paths define the kinds of facts the graph is meant to hold. For a static graph, MetriKG computes metrics that summarize the current shape. Cohesion asks whether related pieces appear to hold together. Connectivity asks whether the graph provides usable paths across entities rather than disconnected islands. Inheritance depth asks how tall or layered the type hierarchy has become. For an evolving graph, the same kinds of measurements can be repeated across time points. The output is not a prediction or generated answer. It is a profile: a multi-dimensional record that supports classification, comparison, and temporal monitoring of graph structure and meaning.
math: The main mathematical idea is measurement of structure. A graph is a mathematical map made of points and links. In this paper, the points are knowledge-graph entities or schema elements, and the links are factual relations or organizing relations such as class inheritance. Once the graph is seen as a map, quality questions become measurable questions. Connectivity counts whether paths exist between places on the map and how fragmented the map is. Cohesion measures whether pieces that should belong together form tight regions instead of being scattered. Inheritance depth measures a hierarchy by counting how many parent-child layers separate general categories from specific ones. Temporal monitoring adds a sequence idea: the same measurements are taken at different moments so change itself becomes something that can be compared. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. A metric deliberately compresses a huge graph into a number or small set of numbers, which makes comparison possible but can hide the local reason behind a change. The math fits MetriKG because graph maintainers need repeatable, comparable signals of structure, not only hand inspection or isolated examples.
dots: MetriKG sits in the repo's knowledge-graph family because it handles the trust problem behind connected facts. Many neighboring papers use knowledge graphs for question answering, recommendation, retrieval, rule mining, causal explanation, or dynamic reasoning. Those systems depend on the graph being coherent enough that following links gives useful evidence rather than confusion. MetriKG does not itself retrieve answers or complete missing facts; it profiles the map those methods may rely on. It is especially close to temporal knowledge graph reasoning papers such as DSTAG and Dual History Enhancement, which treat facts as changing over time. Those papers ask how to predict or reason from change, while MetriKG asks how to measure and monitor the changing graph itself. It also connects to the network concept in the repo: links carry evidence only when the map's structure is meaningful. Profiling is the quality-control branch of the same broader problem.
ww: The approach works because many graph failures leave structural traces before they appear as obvious wrong answers. If a graph becomes fragmented, connectivity measures can reveal that users or downstream systems may no longer travel smoothly from one area of knowledge to another. If related entities stop forming cohesive regions, the graph may be mixing sources, relations, or categories in a way that weakens interpretation. If inheritance depth grows sharply, the schema may be becoming more complex, which can help precision but can also make the graph harder to understand and maintain. Tracking both data and schema matters because the two layers can disagree. Data may expand while the schema stagnates, or the schema may change while old data remains shaped by earlier assumptions. Repeating these measurements over time turns maintenance into comparison: instead of relying on a person's memory of the graph, MetriKG gives a consistent set of signals that can show drift, growth, fragmentation, or reorganization.
po: The payoff is a practical monitoring tool for people who build or maintain knowledge graphs. MetriKG gives them a web-based way to evaluate graphs from RDF files or SPARQL endpoints and inspect multiple dimensions of graph health, including cohesion, connectivity, and inheritance depth. That enables systematic profiling of a single graph, classification of graphs by structural and semantic properties, and temporal monitoring as graphs evolve. The abstract also says the application is open-source and publicly available, which matters because profiling tools are most useful when teams can inspect, reuse, and adapt them to their own graph stores.
limits: The abstract establishes what MetriKG computes, but it does not prove that the chosen metrics catch every important quality problem. A graph can score well on connectivity while containing wrong facts, stale relations, or misleading links. A schema can have reasonable inheritance depth while still using unclear class names or domain assumptions. The method assumes that RDF files or SPARQL endpoints expose enough of the graph and schema to measure them faithfully. It also assumes repeated snapshots are comparable over time. The abstract does not specify evaluation datasets, user studies, runtime costs, or thresholds for deciding when a metric value is good or bad.
